name: Fluoxymesterone

card.summary: Halotestin: a strong oral androgen from the 1950s that bodybuilders add for hardness and aggression; documented trials are in breast cancer and hypogonadism, none in appearance.
card.note: 17-alpha-alkylated oral androgen; liver and mood effects discussed by forum users and in clinical literature.

quick.overview:
Fluoxymesterone, sold as Halotestin, is an oral androgen first described in the 1950s. In medicine it was used for male hypogonadism and delayed puberty, and as palliative hormone therapy for advanced breast cancer. In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a strong, short-acting oral for strength, hardness and aggression rather than for size.

Published trials of the drug are in breast cancer and anemia, not in physique or facial appearance. One looksmax.org poster described planning a regimen with a growth-hormone secretagogue and asked about liver protection.
quick.mechanism: It is a testosterone derivative with a fluorine atom and 17-alpha methyl group that allow oral use and strong androgenic activity; Grokipedia describes it as androgen-receptor mediated with high androgenic potency relative to its anabolic effect.[1][2]
quick.risks: Forum users and one literature summary link long-term use of 17-alpha-alkylated androgens such as fluoxymesterone to hepatocellular adenomas, jaundice and lipid changes, and users describe aggression as a reported effect.[3][4][5] Medical use has declined, and US brand production reportedly ceased in 2014.[1]

lead: Fluoxymesterone (brand name Halotestin; also Androxy) is a synthetic oral androgen and anabolic steroid derived from testosterone. A 1957 JAMA article already carried its name, and later literature describes its use as a replacement androgen in hypogonadism and, in women, as hormone therapy for advanced breast cancer.[6][2][7]

Randomized trials compared it with or added it to tamoxifen and chemotherapy in metastatic breast cancer, and a trial compared androgens for anemia in hemodialysis patients.[8][9][10][11] Reviews also note that high doses of synthetic androgens including fluoxymesterone are given by athletes.[2]

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities it is discussed as a potent oral for hardness, strength and drive; users also discuss its liver toxicity and tendency to produce aggression, and one looksmax.org poster described pairing a small dose with MK-677.[12][13][5] No published study has tested it for cosmetic or physique outcomes.

paras: Reviews list fluoxymesterone, along with methyltestosterone, among oral androgens used as replacement therapy for hypogonadism; the same review states that use in idiopathic male infertility and in erectile dysfunction in elderly men was less effective.[2] Pediatric literature from the 1960s discussed the clinical use and specific dangers of anabolic steroids in children.[14] Grokipedia also reports use for delayed puberty.[1]

In breast cancer, a 1980 controlled trial and a 1988 randomized trial studied tamoxifen alone or combined with fluoxymesterone in postmenopausal women with metastatic disease, and the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group trial E3186 randomized 231 patients to chemotherapy with or without tamoxifen plus Halotestin.[9][8][10] Review articles on adjuvant and metastatic breast cancer therapy discuss the place of androgens.[15][7][16] Fluoxymesterone was one of the androgens compared for anemia in hemodialysis patients in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1981.[11] A registered phase 2 trial of androgen therapy in receptor-negative metastatic breast cancer was terminated after enrolling 5 patients.[17]

On looksmax.org, one user describing a plan to ascend again said he intended to take a low daily amount of Halotestin together with MK-677 and asked about timing and whether liver-support supplements were needed.[12] On T Nation, posters describe it as taken before lifting by some strength users and as a compound used for strength gains rather than mass; another says certain anabolic steroids, fluoxymesterone among them, have been used to stimulate growth in height in short children before growth plates close.[18][19] None of these claims has been tested in a published trial.

Clinical studies are in oncology and hematology: randomized trials of tamoxifen with or without fluoxymesterone in metastatic breast cancer, the ECOG E3186 chemo-hormonal trial in 231 patients and a comparison of androgens for anemia in hemodialysis; a registered trial in receptor-negative breast cancer was terminated with 5 patients.[8][9][10][11][17] No study has tested it for physique or appearance.

A T Nation poster described oral steroids like Halotestin as raising free testosterone relative to total testosterone with more side effects and liver damage and said jaundice is easy to trigger.[4] Another cited literature on prolonged use of methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone and related 17-alpha-alkylated androgens showing hepatocellular adenomas that were not uncommon.[20][3] Posters also name it among compounds that can make users aggressive, and describe a 'flatness' feeling associated with strong androgens.[13][5]

One poster raised the question of whether fluoxymesterone might influence cortisol metabolism and immune function, citing rodent and in-vitro literature; this was speculation rather than study data.[21]

Fluoxymesterone is a synthetic androgen with a fluorine atom at the 9-alpha position and a 17-alpha methyl group. A radioimmunoassay for the drug was published in 1975, and Grokipedia describes oral tablets only, with brand production in the United States ending in 2014.[22][1]

A T Nation poster in 2018 noted that oxandrolone, oxymetholone, fluoxymesterone and methyltestosterone still existed on the US market, assuming prescriptions would be for wasting disease or bodybuilding.[23] A T Nation thread about reference-book warnings in the Physicians' Desk Reference mentions Halotestin alongside other steroid brands.[24]

timeline.event: JAMA publishes a note on fluoxymesterone.[6]
A controlled trial compares tamoxifen and fluoxymesterone in advanced breast cancer.[9]
The New England Journal of Medicine publishes a comparison of androgens for anemia in hemodialysis.[11]
A randomized trial of tamoxifen alone or combined with fluoxymesterone in postmenopausal metastatic breast cancer is published.[8]

lore.intro: Halotestin is discussed on forums as a short-acting oral for strength, hardness and drive, with recurring comments on liver toxicity and aggression.[12][13][5]

claims.claim: Halotestin adds hardness and strength more than size.
claims.believers: Posters describe a flat, hard feel and strength use, and one describes a user lifting after taking it.[18][13]
claims.experts: No published study has measured physique or strength outcomes of fluoxymesterone in healthy people; the literature is clinical.[2][8]

claims.believers: T Nation members list it among compounds they say are prone to causing aggression.[5]
claims.experts: No published trial of fluoxymesterone examining behavior or aggression in healthy people was located.

claims.claim: Oral fluoxymesterone is hard on the liver.
claims.believers: Users cite jaundice risk and literature on hepatocellular adenomas with prolonged 17-alpha-alkylated steroid use.[3][4]
claims.experts: Grokipedia lists hepatotoxicity from C17-alpha alkylation; no dedicated published liver study of fluoxymesterone in users was located.[1]

claims.claim: Some anabolic steroids, fluoxymesterone included, can promote height gain in short children.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster notes use of anabolic steroids to stimulate linear growth in short children before plates fuse.[19]
claims.experts: Pediatric literature reviewed the clinical use and specific dangers of anabolic steroids in children; no evidence addresses use for height in healthy teens.[14]
